book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail

chapters.relation: In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.

Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.

Jack Stillwaggon recounts his 1965 voyage as a seventeen-year-old crewing the replica HMS Bounty from New York to Florida — fires aboard, thirty-five-foot seas, seasickness, a crewman nearly left to die — and asks why modern people abandon comfort to court danger and discomfort. His answer is that we face the sea to prove something to ourselves about our worth and abilities: like the paratrooper who stays under fire or the soldier earning his 'red badge of courage,' the survived ordeal becomes a cherished high point that adds meaning to an otherwise 'silly' comfortable existence, leaving him more at peace and expecting more of himself thereafter.

Gary Jobson, writing from a long racing career with no philosophical vocabulary, offers practical wisdom on generating the inner strength and courage to win: focus on the task at hand rather than the outcome, visualize the race, stay calm under adversity, and 'have fun.' Through stories of Buddy Melges, Ted Turner's Fastnet, and Dennis Conner's America's Cup comeback, plus his own collegiate turnaround under coach Graham Hall, he argues resolve (not luck) drives comebacks, and he treats leadership, mentorship, patience, and consistency as cultivated traits of character — an implicit account of the virtues a competitive sailor must build.

Crista Lebens narrates a C-Scow sail on an inland lake — preparing the boat, casting off, coming about, capsizing, returning to the pier — as a journey toward Aristotelian eudaimonia (human flourishing). She argues sailing demands phronesis (practical wisdom) as body-knowledge, that coming about requires the Greek 'middle path' between being 'in irons' and capsizing, and that competence 'cannot be faked' so sailing forces one to live 'in truth' (via Werth's and Kierkegaard's account of the crowd 'in untruth'). Using Borgmann's device/thing distinction, she casts the sailboat as a 'thing' that calls forth skilled engagement, unlike the powerboat as a 'device' of consumption, and links truth to the beauty of a well-trimmed sail.

Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.

James Whitehill treats sailing his Cape Cod catboat, named Garuda, as a Zen practice modeled on Zen archery (kyudo) and tea ceremony. He organizes it into 'outer work' (technique and ritualized performance) and 'inner work' (cultivating ki energy through breathing and belly-awareness, then 'self-forgetting'), quoting Dogen's dictum that studying the self is forgetting the self, and forgetting the self is being authenticated by all things. The goal is a boat-and-sailor unity in which the sailor 'sails without sailing' — reaching, through mundane repetitive discipline rather than a sought-after peak experience, a nirvana-like state where wind, wave, and self merge.

Gregory and Tod Bassham argue Stoicism is the seaman's philosophy of agency, teaching a clear-eyed grasp of what we can control, influence, or not control at all. Using Epictetus's play metaphor and 'you will fetter my leg but not my will,' Seneca and Marcus Aurelius on fear, they map three techniques onto sailing: cheerful resignation (Gerry Spiess righting Yankee Girl, Shackleton's James Caird crew laughing amid the Southern Ocean), self-sufficiency (splicing lines, emotional independence on a cramped boat), and negative visualization / premeditatio malorum (practicing docking under sail, imagining lost rudders). Skip Allen scuttling Wildflower and Dinelli's endurance illustrate the trichotomy of control and freedom of mind.

Steven Horrobin sorts sailors into three kinds — the cultural-iconography poser, the racer chasing a land-based prize, and the 'sailor of the third kind' for whom the open-ended voyage is an end in itself — and argues the third lives 'in the shadow of Heraclitus.' Against the substantialist ontology of Parmenides and Democritus (persons and boats as fixed things), he defends a process view in which everything, like a wave, is a passing fluctuation of one universal substance; citing Spinoza, self-becoming is the super-process reflecting itself. He dissolves the Ship of Theseus paradox (and Parfit's parallel-ship version) by making identity the continuity of a process's function rather than fixed parts, arguing the violent, corroding life of a boat reveals the flux beneath apparently stable things.

Nicholas Hayes describes the Chicago-to-Mackinac race, cataloguing its boats (passenger trains, Model Ts, booster rockets, retreads), its nights (darkest, stormy, breathless, velvet, brightest), and its sailor-types (tweener, superhero, teammate, yogi, minister, salt) to build toward a claim about an 'awareness shift.' He argues that far from land and its electric lights, sailors slip into a place where the emotional self meets 'the most real and primitive world' and confronts a new relationship with time, culminating on the 'day of hope' in the realization that one controls nothing but oneself and owns nothing but one's time — 'Everything is now' — a transcendence he loosely likens to skepticism and enlightenment themes.

Steve Matthews uses windsurfing to analyze Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' — the loss of self-awareness in skilled action between boredom and anxiety — and argues its intensity comes from 'integration,' where footstraps and harness bind sailor to kit so the equipment becomes 'an extension of oneself.' Invoking Descartes' own admission that mind and body form a unity (not merely pilot in a vessel), he applies Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis: the windsurfer's kit and body form a coupled cognitive system, so 'I' extends to include the gear. He distinguishes true flow from mere goal-satisfaction (rejecting the ocean-cruiser's landfall as flow) and, via Velleman, locates flow's value in intrinsically motivated action that is its own end.

Ilundáin-Agurruza, Gagliardini Graça, and Jáuregui-Olaiz chart sailing's aesthetic facets — sublime, tempestuous, graceful, existential. They deploy Kant's analysis of the sublime as the balance between the imagination's failure before the ocean's immensity/power and the pleasure of meeting it through skill and reason (Ilundáin sailing in thirty-knot gusts on the point of balance between fear and joy). Dewey's notion of 'an experience' anchors sailing's transformative, self-revealing potential, terrifying storms included (Jáuregui's Snowgoose ordeal mistaking a bordello's red light for a harbor). Closing with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, they argue freedom is 'relative' and earned: we cannot change the wind but adjust the sails, gaining restrained autonomy by cultivating skill within constraint.

Jesse Steinberg and Michael Stuckart distinguish instrumental from intrinsic value (using Frankena's list) across sailing's gear, knowledge, and aesthetics, then argue via Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that sailing is a route to eudaimonia through the cultivation of virtue. They show sailing exemplifies courage as the golden mean between cowardice and foolhardiness (deciding whether to go out in twenty-knot winds, judging teen solo circumnavigators), being hard-working (the mean between laziness and workaholism), and cleverness (jury-rigging, navigation). They contend sailing demands a broader, deeper range of virtues than golf, bowling, or power-boating, making it an especially rich — though not the only — path to a flourishing, happy life.

Sebastian Kuhn asks whether Einstein's relativity bears on sailing and answers that its philosophical underpinnings do. He shows sailors constantly juggle multiple reference frames (water, ground, boat, stars) and that Galilean relativity — the laws of nature holding in every inertial frame — suffices to understand tacking, apparent wind, and current, using the example of a boat drifting with a river feeling becalmed. He then explains special relativity's constant speed of light forcing revised notions of simultaneity, length, and time (illustrated with GPS light-pulse timing), and general relativity's curved spacetime (parallel ships meeting at the pole, time running slower low on the mast), noting GPS must correct for both effects to fix a sailor's position.

John D. Norton poses three sailing paradoxes — how a wind-powered boat sails into the wind, faster than the wind, and whether 'making its own wind' makes it a perpetual-motion machine — echoing Zeno's paradoxes of motion and measure as engines of philosophical clarity. He resolves the first two by rejecting the causal truism that an effect cannot exceed or oppose its cause (the wind's force, resolved into drive and beam components against a resistant hull, is the real cause), using this to argue causal principles are elastic labels grafted onto science, never laws it must obey. For the third he builds an idealized wind-turbine boat thought experiment showing created-wind energy is exactly consumed by counter-force, and debates James Brown's Platonist view (that thought experiments 'see' laws in a Platonic realm, like grasping the ideal triangle) against his own deflationary view that they are merely picturesque argument.

Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.

Hilaire Belloc's essay 'The Channel,' serving as the volume's literary epilogue, argues that the 'glamour in the mind' and 'freshness of beginnings' our ancestors knew can be recovered by using the body simply and hardly — best of all by sailing a small boat under twenty-five feet across the Channel. Narrating his own first crossing from the Goodwins to Calais, drifting on the ebb and waiting for the flood, he presents sailing as the 'old drama by which the soul of a healthy man is kept alive,' teaching terror, salvation, exultation, and repose as lived realities rather than mere words. He closes by withholding the tale of the stormy return, imploring readers not to hear of it but to sail it themselves.
